points.title: Large-scale and small-scale maps
points.brief: A large-scale map shows a small area in great detail, and a small-scale map shows a large area with little detail.

points.title: Latitude and longitude
points.brief: Lines of latitude run east to west and measure degrees north or south of the equator. Longitude measures degrees east or west of Greenwich, and both use degrees and minutes.

points.title: The 16-point compass and bearings
points.brief: The 16-point compass adds directions such as NNE and WSW, and a bearing gives direction as an angle from 0 to 360 degrees clockwise from north.

points.title: Calculating distance and area with a ratio scale
points.brief: With a scale such as 1 to 25,000, one centimetre on the map is 250 metres on the ground, and area is found by counting grid squares.

points.title: Local relief and gradient
points.brief: Local relief is the difference between the highest and lowest points in an area. Gradient is the rise over the horizontal distance, written as a ratio such as 1 in 20.

chapters.title: Thematic maps, statistics and spatial data

points.title: Choropleth maps
points.brief: A choropleth map shades areas in darker or lighter colours to show how much of something each area has, such as population density.

points.title: Reading synoptic charts
points.brief: On a synoptic chart, isobars join places of equal air pressure. Close isobars mean strong winds, highs bring fine weather and lows and fronts bring rain.

points.title: Population pyramids
points.brief: A population pyramid shows a country's people by age and sex. A wide base means many young people, and a narrow base with a wide top means an ageing population.

points.title: Scatter plots and correlation
points.brief: A scatter plot shows whether two sets of data are linked, such as income and life expectancy, with a positive, negative or no correlation.

points.title: Steps of a geographical inquiry
points.brief: An inquiry starts with a question and a plan, collects and processes information, draws conclusions, proposes action and then evaluates how well it worked.

points.title: Primary and secondary data
points.brief: Primary data is collected first-hand, such as by surveys and fieldwork. Secondary data comes from others, such as census figures and reports.

points.title: Evaluating an inquiry
points.brief: A good evaluation asks whether the data was reliable and enough, whether sources were biased, and what could be done better next time.

points.title: What a biome is
points.brief: A biome is a large region with a similar climate, soils, plants and animals, such as a desert, tundra or tropical rainforest.

points.title: Where the biomes are
points.brief: Biomes form broad bands across the world, with rainforests near the equator, deserts near the tropics and tundra near the poles.

points.title: Why biomes differ
points.brief: Climate is the main factor, especially temperature and rainfall, along with latitude, altitude, soils and distance from the sea.

points.title: Biomes as a natural resource
points.brief: Biomes provide food, fibres such as cotton and wool, timber, medicines and clean water, and they store carbon.

points.title: Grassland biomes and food
points.brief: Grasslands, such as the Australian rangelands and the North American prairies, are used for grazing and grain growing, but face drought and soil erosion.

points.title: Changing biomes to grow more food
points.brief: People alter biomes to grow food by clearing vegetation, irrigating, terracing slopes, draining wetlands and adding fertilisers.

points.title: Factors in food supply
points.brief: Food supply in Australia and Asia depends on environmental factors such as climate and water, and on land, technology, labour and money.

points.title: Factors in food demand
points.brief: Demand for food grows with population, rising incomes and changing diets, such as more meat and dairy eaten across Asia.

points.title: Environmental impacts of food production
points.brief: Farming can cause land clearing, soil erosion, salinity, water pollution from fertilisers, overuse of rivers and loss of biodiversity.

points.title: What food security is
points.brief: Food security means all people always have enough safe and nutritious food. Food insecurity is when they do not.

points.title: Threats to food security
points.brief: Poverty, conflict, drought, climate change, land degradation, food waste and rising prices all threaten food security.

points.title: Sustainable farming practices
points.brief: Practices such as crop rotation, no-till farming, efficient irrigation and cutting food waste help produce food while protecting land for the future.

points.title: Aboriginal knowledges and food systems
points.brief: Aboriginal Peoples grew, harvested and stored native grains, tubers and seeds for thousands of years, and this knowledge can help build food systems suited to Australia.

points.title: Push and pull factors
points.brief: Push factors, such as war, poverty or disaster, drive people away. Pull factors, such as jobs, safety and family, draw them to a place.

points.title: Types of migration
points.brief: Migration can be internal, within a country, or international, between countries, and voluntary or forced, as for refugees.

points.title: Effects of migration on origin and destination
points.brief: Migrants send money home and fill job gaps where they go, but the place they leave can lose young and skilled workers.

points.title: Migration to Australia
points.brief: People have migrated to Australia from Britain and Europe after World War II, and more recently from Asia, especially China and India.

points.title: Effects of migration on Australia
points.brief: Migration grows Australia's population and workforce, adds cultural diversity and puts pressure on housing and services in big cities.

points.title: Internal migration in Australia
points.brief: Australians move for work, study, retirement and lifestyle, such as sea change and tree change moves to the coast and the country.

points.title: Rural to urban migration in China
points.brief: Hundreds of millions of people in China have moved from farms to cities for factory and service jobs, one of the largest movements in history.

points.title: What urbanisation is
points.brief: Urbanisation is the growing share of a country's people who live in towns and cities rather than in the country.

points.title: Causes and consequences of urbanisation
points.brief: People move to cities for jobs and services. Fast growth can bring traffic, pollution, high housing costs and informal settlements.

points.title: Australia's urban pattern
points.brief: Australia is one of the most urbanised countries, with most people living in a few coastal capital cities.

points.title: Living in urban, rural and remote places
points.brief: Cities offer jobs and services but cost more, while rural and remote places offer space and community but have fewer services.

points.title: Urban sprawl and urban consolidation
points.brief: Urban sprawl spreads houses outward onto farmland and bush. Urban consolidation fits more homes into existing suburbs, such as apartments near transport.

points.title: Sustainable city strategies
points.brief: Cities can become more sustainable with public transport, cycleways, green space, tree cover, energy-efficient buildings and less waste.

points.title: Managing population growth in Sydney
points.brief: Sydney manages growth with new suburbs in the west, higher density near train lines, and new transport such as the Metro, with different views from residents, councils and developers.

points.title: Planning with Country and diverse communities
points.brief: Planning for diverse communities includes Aboriginal knowledges of caring for Country, such as restoring waterways and native plants in new suburbs.

points.title: The functions of environments
points.brief: Environments provide resources, absorb and break down waste, and support life through services such as clean air, water and pollination.

points.title: Natural processes that change environments
points.brief: Natural processes such as weather, erosion, fire, floods and plate movement change environments over time.

points.title: Human-induced environmental change
points.brief: People change environments through land clearing, pollution, introduced species, dams and burning fossil fuels that cause climate change.

points.title: Consequences of environmental change
points.brief: Environmental change can cause loss of biodiversity and habitat, degraded soil and water, more extreme weather and harm to people's livelihoods.

points.title: Perspectives on managing environments
points.brief: Governments, farmers, developers, scientists, environmental groups and Aboriginal communities can hold different views on how an environment should be used.

points.title: Aboriginal custodianship of Country
points.brief: Aboriginal custodianship sees people as responsible for caring for Country, through practices such as cultural burning and the work of Indigenous rangers.

points.title: Prevention, mitigation and preparedness
points.brief: Prevention stops harm before it starts, mitigation reduces its effects, and preparedness gets people ready to respond when it happens.

points.title: Judging whether management is sustainable
points.brief: Management can be judged on whether it protects the environment, is fair to people and pays its way, now and for future generations.

points.title: Coastal processes
points.brief: Waves, tides, currents and wind shape coasts, eroding headlands and moving sand along beaches and dunes.

points.title: Threats to coastal environments
points.brief: Coasts are changed by building close to the shore, rising sea levels, storm erosion, pollution and loss of dune plants.

points.title: Managing coasts
points.brief: Coasts are managed with sea walls and groynes, adding sand to beaches, replanting dunes and planning rules that keep buildings back.

points.title: Comparing coasts in Australia and another country
points.brief: Coastal towns in Australia and low-lying countries such as Bangladesh face rising seas, but their wealth shapes how they can respond.

points.title: Rivers and wetlands as environments
points.brief: Rivers, lakes and wetlands store and filter water, support fish and birds, and are linked to the land around them through their catchments.

points.title: Changes to the Murray-Darling Basin
points.brief: Dams, weirs and taking water for irrigation in the Murray-Darling Basin have reduced flows, causing salinity, algal blooms and fish deaths.

points.title: Managing inland water
points.brief: The Murray-Darling Basin Plan sets limits on water taken and returns water to the environment, with irrigators, towns and First Nations groups holding different views.

points.title: Comparing inland water in Australia and another country
points.brief: Rivers shared by several regions or countries, such as the Mekong, face the same competing uses as the Murray-Darling, managed in different ways.

points.title: Human wellbeing
points.brief: Human wellbeing is the quality of people's lives, including health, education, income, safety, freedom and a clean environment.

points.title: Human Development Index
points.brief: The Human Development Index combines life expectancy, years of schooling and income per person to rank countries' development.

points.title: Other measures of wellbeing
points.brief: Wellbeing is also measured by GDP per person, infant mortality, literacy, access to clean water and how satisfied people say they are.

points.title: Global patterns of wellbeing
points.brief: Wellbeing is highest in places such as Western Europe, North America and Australia, and lowest in parts of sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.

points.title: Global challenges to wellbeing
points.brief: Poverty, conflict, disease, climate change and unequal access to education and health care hold back wellbeing in many places.

points.title: Variations within India
points.brief: In India, wellbeing varies between rich and poor states, cities and villages, and social groups, because of income, services and history.

points.title: Location and wellbeing in Australia
points.brief: In Australia, wellbeing tends to be lower in remote places, with fewer jobs, health services and schools than in the cities.

points.title: Factors behind variations in wellbeing
points.brief: Environmental, economic, social and technological factors, such as climate, jobs, education and internet access, explain why wellbeing varies.

points.title: Closing the Gap
points.brief: Closing the Gap is an agreement between governments and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander organisations with targets for health, education and jobs.

points.title: Government initiatives
points.brief: Governments improve wellbeing through health care, schooling, welfare payments and building infrastructure such as water and roads.

points.title: Non-government organisations and aid
points.brief: Charities and aid groups, such as the Red Cross, and foreign aid from countries such as Australia fund projects in health, water and education.

points.title: Perspectives on wellbeing initiatives
points.brief: People judge initiatives differently, such as whether aid reaches those in need and whether local people had a say in it.

points.title: Aboriginal Community Controlled Organisations
points.brief: Aboriginal Community Controlled Organisations are run by local Aboriginal communities and deliver health and other services in culturally safe ways.
